'''Dajuan Marquett Wagner Sr.''' (born February 4, 1983) is an American former professional [[basketball]] player. He is the son of former [[University of Louisville]] and [[National Basketball Association]] player [[Milt Wagner]]<ref name=WarriorsSign/> and left the NBA early into his career because of debilitating health problems. He was drafted sixth overall by the [[Cleveland Cavaliers]] in the [[2002 NBA draft]].

==High school career==
Wagner attended [[Camden High School (New Jersey)|Camden High School]], where he played with the varsity team freshman year. He debuted on December 19, 1997, against Highland High School, scoring 12 points. He went on to play in 27 games his first season, averaging 27.3 points and recording a season-high of 45 points against [[Red Bank Catholic High School|Red Bank]] on February 13, 1998,<ref name=camden>{{Cite news|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/14762697/dajuan_wagners_career_at_camden_nj/|title=Dajuan Wagner game-by-game|newspaper=[[Courier-Post]]|date=March 17, 2001|page=58}}</ref> and at the end of the season he received the Freshman of the Year award from [[ESPN]].<ref name=underclass>{{Cite news|url=http://www.espn.co.uk/high-school/boys-basketball/story/_/id/7793355/all-time-underclass-poys|title=All-time underclass POYs|author=Flores, Ronnie|date=May 18, 2001|publisher=[[ESPN]].co.uk|access-date=March 17, 2019}}</ref> In his sophomore year, Dajuan played in 17 games and had a new career-high of 57 points against [[Camden County Technical Schools Pennsauken Campus|Pennsauken Tech]] on January 26. He finished the season averaging 35.3 points per game,<ref name=camden /> and won the ESPN Sophomore of the Year award.<ref name=underclass />

The following year he played in 28 games. On January 31, 2000, he scored 80 points (24 of which in the fourth quarter) in a 122–66 win against Pennsauken Tech.<ref name=camden /><ref name=score>{{Cite news|title=Dajuan Wagner scores 80|newspaper=[[The Courier-Journal]]|date=February 2, 2000|page=12}}</ref> In his junior year he was already considered one of the top players of his class.<ref name=score /><ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.espn.com/recruiting/s/2000/0508/522333.html|title=Stevenson headed to NBA|date=May 8, 2000|author=Hodge, Bill|work=ESPN.com|access-date=March 17, 2019}}</ref> At the end of the season he had an average of 31.9 points per game.<ref name=camden /> For his senior year he debuted on December 15 scoring 36 points against [[Eastern Regional High School|Eastern]], followed by a 50-points performance against [[Bishop Eustace Preparatory School|Bishop Eustace]].<ref name=camden />

On January 16, 2001, he [[List of basketball players who have scored 100 points in a single game|scored 100 points]] against Camden County Tech. He converted 42 of his 61 field goals (with 10 3-pointers) and 6 free throws: he scored 25 points in the first quarter, 21 in the second, 26 in the third and 28 in the fourth.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.philly.com/philly/sports/sixers/20120302_Camden_s_Dajuan_Wagner_still_hears_about_his_100-point_game_in_2001.html|title=Camden's Dajuan Wagner still hears about his 100-point game in 2001|publisher=[[philly.com]]|author=Narducci, Marc|date=March 2, 2012|access-date=March 17, 2019}}</ref> He went on to score 50 or more points 4 more times during the season, and averaged 42.5 points in 29 games played as a senior.<ref name=camden /> He scored 3,462 points in high school (the most in New Jersey high school history, breaking former high school star John Somogyi's scoring record of 3,451 points; when Somogyi played there was no 3-point shot), and scored 25 points in the [[2001 McDonald's All-American Boys Game|McDonald's All-American Game]].<ref>Strauss, Robert. [https://www.nytimes.com/2000/02/13/nyregion/in-person-hoop-dreams-revisit-camden.html " IN PERSON; Hoop Dreams Revisit Camden"], ''[[The New York Times]]'', February 13, 2000. Accessed April 6, 2008.</ref> Wagner is considered by many to be the greatest high school basketball player in New Jersey history.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://fanmonster.com/?p=4273|title=Cleveland Browns NFL Football|access-date=July 11, 2016}}</ref><ref name="philly.com">[http://www.philly.com/philly/sports/sportsweek/20120129_Whatever_happened_to_Dajuan_Wagner_.html Philadelphia local news, sports, jobs, cars, homes – Philly.com] {{webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121010183335/http://www.philly.com/philly/sports/sportsweek/20120129_Whatever_happened_to_Dajuan_Wagner_.html |date=October 10, 2012 }}</ref>

==College career==
Wagner considered offers from [[Connecticut Huskies men's basketball|Connecticut]], [[Kentucky Wildcats men's basketball|Kentucky]], [[Louisville Cardinals men's basketball|Louisville]], [[Memphis Tigers men's basketball|Memphis]] and [[Miami Hurricanes men's basketball|Miami (FL)]],<ref>{{Cite news|title=POTENTIAL RECRUITS|date=May 27, 2000|newspaper=The Courier-Journal|page=16}}</ref> and signed with Memphis in June 2000.<ref>{{Cite news|author=Kriegel, Mark|title=NCAA knows it's all relative|newspaper=Daily News|date=June 23, 2000}}</ref>
He played one year of [[college basketball]] at the [[University of Memphis]]. He scored a season-high 32 points against [[Old Dominion Monarchs basketball|Old Dominion]] on November 14, 2001, in his 2nd game with Memphis, and tied his season high on March 26, 2002, against [[Temple Owls men's basketball|Temple]] during the [[2002 National Invitation Tournament|NIT]] semifinal.<ref name=draft>{{Cite web|url=https://www.nba.com/draft2002/profiles/dajuan_wagner.html|title=Dajuan Wagner|work=NBA.com|date=2002|access-date=March 19, 2019}}</ref> He contributed with 16 points in the title game win against [[South Carolina Gamecocks men's basketball|South Carolina]] and at the end of the season he earned several NIT and conference honors, including the MVP award of the 2002 NIT. He also broke the record for points in a single season for Memphis with 762.<ref name=draft />

His coach, [[John Calipari]], revoked Wagner's scholarship after his freshman year to force him to enter the NBA, because Calipari believed that Wagner should not avoid the money he would receive as a first-round draft pick.<ref name="king20090317
">{{cite news | url=https://sports.yahoo.com/ncaa/basketball/news?slug=jn-calipari031709 | title=Just win, baby | access-date=March 9, 2011 | author=King, Jason | date=March 17, 2009 | publisher=Yahoo! Sports}}</ref><ref name="price20110314">{{cite magazine | url=http://cnnsi.printthis.clickability.com/pt/cpt?expire=&title=The+NCAA+hasn%27t+held+him+accountable+for+any+major+-+03.14.11+-+SI+Vault&urlID=448405447&action=cpt&partnerID=289881&fb=Y&url=http://sportsillustrated.cnn.com/vault/article/magazine/MAG1182972/index.htm | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110313081950/http://cnnsi.printthis.clickability.com/pt/cpt?expire=&title=The+NCAA+hasn%27t+held+him+accountable+for+any+major+-+03.14.11+-+SI+Vault&urlID=448405447&action=cpt&partnerID=289881&fb=Y&url=http://sportsillustrated.cnn.com/vault/article/magazine/MAG1182972/index.htm | url-status=dead | archive-date=March 13, 2011 | title=Too Slick, Too Loud, Too Successful Why John Calipari Can't Catch A Break | access-date=March 9, 2011 | author=Price, S. ==Professional career==

=== Cleveland Cavaliers (2002–2005) ===
Wagner was chosen with the sixth overall pick of the [[2002 NBA draft]] by the [[Cleveland Cavaliers]]. In his rookie season he averaged 13.4 points per game and shot 36.9% from the field.

Wagner was hampered by injuries and health problems thereafter. He averaged a career-low 4.0 points in 11 games played during the [[2004–05 NBA season|2004–05 season]], and was hospitalized for [[ulcerative colitis]]. The Cavaliers did not exercise their option on his contract for the [[2005–06 NBA season|2005–06 season]] and subsequently Wagner was out of the league.

=== Golden State Warriors (2006) ===
Wagner's colitis condition was not amenable to medication and, after consulting with [[New York Knicks]] head coach [[Larry Brown (basketball)|Larry Brown]], who referred him to a New York medical expert, he underwent surgery to remove half his colon on October 25, 2005, at [[Mount Sinai Hospital, New York|Mount Sinai Hospital]].

On September 22, 2006, Wagner signed a two-year $1.6 million contract with the [[Golden State Warriors]].<ref name=WarriorsSign>{{cite web|url=https://www.espn.com/nba/news/story?id=2598975|title=Wagner signs with Warriors after two years out of NBA|date=September 22, 2006|access-date=July 11, 2016}}</ref> On November 20, two months after he recovered from a serious illness to make an NBA comeback, the Warriors bought out his contract after he had played one game for the team.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.espn.com/nba/news/story?id=2669233|title=Tryout over: Warriors release little-used guard Wagner|date=November 21, 2006|access-date=July 11, 2016}}</ref> That one game that Wagner played with Golden State ended up being the only game he played in the 2006–2007 season and the final game of his NBA career. The game was played on November 11, 2006, with the Warriors defeating the [[Detroit Pistons]] 111–79. Wagner recorded 4 points and 1 assist.

=== Prokom Trefl Sopot (2007) ===
On August 31, 2007, Wagner signed a one-year contract with [[Prokom Trefl Sopot]] in Poland.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.euroleague.net/news/i/15182/180/item|title=Prokom signs point guard Wagner|access-date=July 11, 2016}}</ref><ref>[http://www.prokom.trefl.com.pl/index2.php?page=eng&id=3098 Dajuan Wagner in Prokom Trefl!] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070907082148/http://www.prokom.trefl.com.pl/index2.php?page=eng |date=September 7, 2007 }} August 31, 2007</ref> Averaging 8.3 points in six games, he returned to South Jersey after hurting his hip and reinjuring his knee in Poland.

On October 12, 2015, he attempted to return to basketball and planned to sign with the AmeriLeague.<ref>{{cite news|title=Dajuan Wagner Continues Comeback — Signs With AmeriLeague |url=http://www.amerileague.com/blog/dajuan-wagner-continues-comeback-signs-with-amerileague/ |access-date=October 12, 2015 |work=AmeriLeague.com |date=October 12, 2015 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151016163555/http://www.amerileague.com/blog/dajuan-wagner-continues-comeback-signs-with-amerileague/ |archive-date=October 16, 2015 }}</ref> However, the league folded days later, after it was discovered that the founder was a [[con artist]].<ref>{{cite news|title=AmeriLeague Founder Revealed As Con Artist|url=http://basketball.realgm.com/wiretap/239602/AmeriLeague-Founder-Revealed-As-Con-Artist|access-date=October 22, 2015|work=RealGM.com|date=October 22, 2015}}</ref>

Wagner has been a resident of [[West Deptford Township, New Jersey]].<ref>Mannix, Chris. [https://web.archive.org/web/20100828055937/http://sportsillustrated.cnn.com/vault/article/magazine/MAG1108917/index.htm "Intestinal Fortitude; After surgery for colitis, Dajuan Wagner is trying to resume a career that once showed such promise"], ''[[Sports Illustrated]]'', September 11, 2006, backed up by the [[Internet Archive]] as of August 26, 2010. Accessed October 25, 2015.</ref>

==Personal life==
Wagner is the son of [[Milt Wagner]], who was a second-round pick in the [[1986 NBA draft]].

Wagner's son, [[Dajuan Wagner Jr.]], was ranked the No. 6 basketball recruit in the country for the class of 2023, according to [[247Sports]]<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.cbssports.com/college-basketball/news/class-of-2023-recruiting-rankings-headlined-by-dajuan-wagner-jr-mikey-williams-and-bronny-james/|title=Class of 2023 recruiting rankings headlined by DaJuan Wagner Jr., Mikey Williams and Bronny James|date=30 September 2020|publisher=[[CBSSports.com]]|first1=Kyle|last1=Boone}}</ref> and selected as a McDonald's All American in 2023.
